_comment: FACTORtv — CONVERSATIONS between the booth.
This is not the same thing as the reaction crosstalk in overlay_booth's
CROSSTALK_CATS, where Chuck adds a verdict to a call Miles just made.
This is the booth TALKING TO EACH OTHER during honest dead air, which is
the thing that made RacerTV feel like two people in a commentary box
rather than two narrators sharing a microphone.
Each topic is a three-beat exchange:
q    Miles asks Chuck something, by name.
a    Chuck answers. He answers the QUESTION, so answers cannot be
shared between topics — that is what makes it a conversation.
ack  Miles takes it back. Optional; falls back to _ack.
Gates:  when  race phases the topic makes sense in
needs_race  the topic ASSESSES the race so far, so it is not
offered until enough of one has happened (see
overlay_booth._enough_race). 'Who's impressed you?'
on lap two is a question about nothing. Topics about
the circuit, the cars or the weather carry no such
gate: they are true from the first lap.
needs/not  era capabilities, same meaning as the line pools
slots  {a} {b} {drv} leader, {gap}, {laps}, {trk}, {series}
Chuck is an ex-NASCAR Cup champion who raced stock cars 1985-2006. He
answers from that experience and treats single-seaters as an informed
outsider — no first-person claims about open-wheel racing.
A topic may bind answers to a SPECIFIC question via `qa`. Use it for any
question that is not open-ended: a shared answer pool replied to 'Is
Silverstone a driver's track?' with 'Everything, and all at once', which
answers a different question and is what made the booth sound as though
it was not listening to itself. Topics keeping flat q/a lists are ones
where every question is open enough that any answer fits.
_ack: We'll come back to that, I suspect.
Noted — and let's see if the drivers agree with you.
That's why they pay you, Chuck.
Good point. Back to the racing.
Interesting. Keep an eye on it.
I'll take that. And there's the action to prove it.

_note: The circuit topic where the ANSWER is real. {fact} is filled from
tracks.json for the circuit actually being raced, so Chuck says
something true about this specific place rather than something
generic about places in general. The booth skips this topic entirely
when it does not recognise the circuit — which is the correct
behaviour, and the reason the answers are all pure {fact}.
q: Give us some history on {trk}, Chuck.
What should people know about {trk}, Chuck?
You've read up on {trk}, Chuck — anything for us?
Tell me something about this place, Chuck.
{trk} has a bit of a reputation, doesn't it Chuck?
What's the story of this circuit, Chuck?
a: {fact}
Well — {fact}
Here's the thing about this place. {fact}
Funny you ask. {fact}
This one I do know. {fact}

q: Chuck, who's been the standout for you so far?
Give me a name, Chuck — who's impressed you this afternoon?
Anyone catching your eye out there, Chuck?
a: {drv}, and it isn't close. No drama, no mistakes, just lap after lap.
I'd say {drv}. Nobody's talking about him and he's exactly where he needs to be.
{drv}. He's making the hard overtakes look like nothing at all.
For me it's {drv} — quiet, tidy, and quick where it costs other people time.

qa.q: Are the tyres going to decide this one, Chuck?
a: No question. Whoever's been kindest to the rears wins this.
They usually do. The one who saved a set is about to look very clever.
Not on their own — but they'll decide who can use the pace they've got.

qa.q: Chuck — how much life is left in those tyres?
a: Not much. You can see it in the entry: the fronts have stopped biting.
Enough for now. It's the last third of the run where it gets ugly.
More than you'd think. This surface is kinder than it looks.

qa.q: Talk to me about tyre management, Chuck.
a: It's the whole job. Everyone's quick on new rubber; almost nobody is on old.
In a Cup car you'd nurse them for thirty laps then use everything. Same principle here, shorter fuse.
The driver half a tenth slower every lap is the one still going at the end.

q: Where's this race being won and lost, Chuck?
Chuck, what's the decisive bit of this circuit today?
Where do you have to be brave here, Chuck?
a: On the brakes. Everyone's quick in a straight line; not everyone stops late twice in a row.
Traction on the slow-corner exits. That's where the lap time is hiding.
The middle sector. Whoever commits there is finding half a second and nobody's matching it.
It's the in-lap and the out-lap. Races here are decided on the two laps nobody watches.

qa.q: How much pressure is {drv} under right now, Chuck?
a: Enormous. Leading is the loneliest job in racing and there's no hiding from a mirror.
More than the gap suggests. He knows exactly who's behind him.
Plenty — but he's earned the right to feel it.
I think he can. The braking points haven't moved once, and that's the tell.
For a while. Whether it lasts to the end is a different question.
Yes, if nobody forces the issue. The moment somebody does, we find out.

qa.q: Is the pressure telling on {drv}, do you think?
a: Not yet. He's still hitting the same marks lap after lap.
A little. He's a fraction later on the brakes than he was, and that's how it starts.
You'd never know it from here. That's what experience buys you.

qa.q: Has {drv} got enough in hand, Chuck?
a: Just about. He's responded every single time he's been asked to.
It'll be desperately close. The tyres are fading and {b} knows it.
On this evidence, yes — but he cannot afford one mistake.

qa.q: Chuck — is {drv} going to hold on here?
a: I think so. He's got the pace, and I believe he's got the nerve.
If he keeps it clean, yes. One error and that door swings wide open.
It's going to go to the flag either way.

qa.q: {gap} the gap, Chuck. Is that enough?
a: Not on its own. He needs it to stay there for another ten minutes.
It's enough if he keeps responding. It is not enough to relax with.
Barely. That's inside a mistake, and everybody makes one eventually.

q: Called it yet, Chuck? Who wins this?
Give me a winner, Chuck.
Chuck — how does this finish?
a: {drv}, but not comfortably. He'll be looking at his mirrors for the last ten minutes.
I'm not calling it. Races like this turn on one lap and we haven't had that lap yet.
{drv} on merit. Unless somebody does something silly, and somebody usually does.
The one who's saved something. Right now I genuinely couldn't tell you who that is.

q: What's the strategy call here, Chuck?
Chuck — is the undercut on?
How would you play this from the pit wall, Chuck?
a: Track position, every time. You can't overtake here, so you don't give the place up in the first place.
The undercut is live and it's worth about a second. Somebody's going to blink.
Stay out. Clean air is worth more than fresh rubber on this circuit.
I'd have gone a lap earlier. Once you're in traffic the whole plan belongs to somebody else.

q: That's proper racecraft, isn't it Chuck?
Chuck, how do you actually make a pass stick here?
What separates the good overtakers, Chuck?
a: Patience. You set a pass up two corners before you make it, and everybody who's in a hurry gets it wrong.
You have to be alongside before the apex or you're just a passenger.
Show them the car early, then go somewhere else. Works in a stock car, works here.
The great ones make the other driver make the mistake. They don't force anything.

q: What do you make of these cars, Chuck?
Chuck — how much harder are these than they look?
Would you have fancied one of these, Chuck?
a: Far harder than they look from here. Everything happens at twice the speed I'm used to.
I raced heavy cars with no grip and a lot of banking. This is a different sport with the same steering wheel.
I'd have loved a go. I'd also have been two seconds off and very honest about it.
The braking is what would get me. In a Cup car you're on the pedal for an age; here it's a stab and it's done.

q: What's going through the mind of a leader right now, Chuck?
Chuck — how do you settle yourself at this stage?
Last few laps, Chuck. What does that feel like?
a: Nothing. That's the trick. The second you start thinking about the trophy, you've lost it.
Your hands get tight and the car feels worse than it is. Every driver out there knows that feeling.
You count corners, not laps. Laps are too big a number when you're that close.
You breathe, and you drive the same lap you drove an hour ago. Easy to say.

q: What are they saying on the pit wall, Chuck?
Chuck — what's the radio traffic like at this stage?
What would you be telling your driver right now, Chuck?
a: Almost nothing. The best thing an engineer can do at this point is stay off the radio.
Gaps and nothing else. He doesn't need encouragement, he needs numbers.
I'd tell him the car behind is on older tyres. True or not, it's the only thing worth saying.
They'll be watching the fuel more than the fight. It's the thing that ends races quietly.

qa.q: How would you rate this field, Chuck?
a: Deep. Nobody out there is making up the numbers, which is rarer than it sounds.
Strong at the front, honest behind. That's a healthy grid.
You can see who's raced properly and who's learning. Both are quick; only one is repeatable.

qa.q: Chuck — is this as close as it looks from up here?
a: Closer. When the top ten are covered by a second, one mistake costs five places.
It really is. There's nothing between them on pace.
Closer than it's been all season, and it's making for a good watch.

qa.q: What do you make of the depth of this {series} grid?
a: The front three are on another level, but behind them it's genuinely anybody's.
Deeper than the results suggest. Plenty of them could win on the right day.
It's the middle of the field that impresses me. No easy afternoons in there.

qa.q: What does {trk} ask of a driver, Chuck?
a: Everything, and all at once. There's no corner here where you can have a rest.
Commitment, mostly. The quick way round is the frightening way round.
Precision. It gives you nothing back if you're a foot out of position.

qa.q: Chuck — how much does this circuit punish a mistake?
a: Immediately. Run wide here and you don't lose a tenth, you lose the place.
Enormously. There's no run-off worth the name at the quick bits.
Less than it looks, actually — you can tidy one up if you're quick about it.
Absolutely. You can hide a bad car round here if the driver's brave enough.
It is. The good ones find half a second the rest simply cannot.
More than most. This is a circuit where the man matters more than the machine.

q: What's the weather doing out there, Chuck?
Chuck — how much is the track temperature mattering today?
Is the surface changing, Chuck?
a: It's mattering enormously. A hot track hurts the rear tyre first, and everybody out there is managing that whether they admit it or not.
The surface is cooling, which suits whoever's been struggling for rear grip and hurts whoever's been living off front end.
Track temperature moves the balance more than any setup change these teams have got left. It is the biggest variable of the day.
Enough to matter. A green track and a rubbered-in one are two different circuits, and they arrive four hours apart.

q: Would you have fancied a go in these, Chuck?
Chuck, how would you have got on in one of these?
What do you make of this kind of racing, Chuck?
a: Honestly? I would be quick enough in a straight line and hopeless everywhere else. This is a discipline you learn young or you do not learn.
I have a lot of respect for it. There is nowhere to hide - no aero to lean on, no horsepower to cover a mistake, just what the driver does.
I would enjoy it enormously and I would be beaten by teenagers, which is the correct outcome and would not stop me entering.
The good ones out here are learning things I spent a decade unlearning. This is where a racing driver is actually made.
